text: Hello, it’s Grete. Uncle Henrik comes home from the sea, and something isn’t quite right. A relative nobody has ever mentioned has died, and there will be a casket in the living room. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 8, and draft more of your essay. Today’s question: what is really going on at Uncle Henrik’s house?

Today’s reading move asks you to weigh courage. When several people are brave in the same chapter, ask what each one could lose. A grown-up and a child might both be brave, but the cost isn’t always the same. Look for the details that show you what’s at stake.

The model is a short sentence about Uncle Henrik. The sentence to fix is about a name nobody recognizes. That name has a title in front of it, and the title needs capitals and a small joining mark. And again, two sentences need to be split apart.

This is review, so some of what you see is already right. In grammar and spelling, only tap what needs fixing. Read every line twice before you decide. A good editor knows when to change something, and also when to leave it alone.

This is the last stretch of water. Four more words, and the beam can finally reach the far shore. One of these words describes someone who believes things too easily. As you read, ask whether anyone in this chapter is hoping someone will believe a story.

Last match of the week. See if you can do it with no misses at all. Then try something harder: use two of the words together in one sentence about Annemarie at the house by the sea. Discreet and tense might make a good pair.

Here’s a little draft with some mistakes and some sentences that are fine. Read each one quietly to yourself. Your ear usually knows before your brain can name the rule. Tap only the sentences that sound wrong, then fix one of them.

Six built words, and only some are misspelled. For each one, take it apart: the base, the piece at the front, the piece at the end. Then check each part on its own. Usually only one part has gone wrong.

Today’s Courage Watch is about keeping quiet. Annemarie can tell something about this family story doesn’t add up. She doesn’t argue. She watches. When I was a girl, I learned that sometimes the bravest person in the room is a child who notices everything and says nothing until it’s safe.

Uncle Henrik is a fisherman, and he talks a lot about the weather. Listen to the phrases he uses. Have you heard one of them before? Then pay close attention near the end of the chapter, when Annemarie hears a name she doesn’t know. Notice what she thinks, and what she says out loud.

Now you write. The questions ask why the news of a death seems strange, what an odd phrase about fishing might mean, and what Annemarie begins to suspect. Then you’ll draft a second body paragraph, with a new reason and a new piece of evidence.

For the second question, think back to the phone call in Chapter 6. Where else have you heard grown-ups talk about fishing weather? You don’t have to be sure what it means. A good guess, backed up by what you noticed, is exactly what a careful reader does.

Two reasons are stronger than one. This paragraph has the same shape as the last one: reason, evidence, link. But it needs a brand-new reason and a brand-new quote. If your two paragraphs sound the same, look for a different moment in the book.

I saw a boat like this one years later, in a museum. It’s so small. I stood beside it and tried to picture a dozen people inside, lying still in the dark, listening to the engine and the waves. Some of them were children. I think about the fishermen, too, who did this night after night, and went back to fishing in the morning.

This card belongs to Dr. Karl Henry Køster, a surgeon at Bispebjerg Hospital in Copenhagen. In October 1943, he and the nurses and doctors there hid Jewish families among their patients, and in the hospital chapel. One day, a long funeral line of taxis drove away from that chapel. The people inside weren’t going to a funeral. They were families on their way to the boats.
Credulous. Too quick to believe things.
Creditor. Someone who trusts you to pay them back.
Tendency. A leaning toward something, like a habit.
Superintendent. The person who watches over a school or a building. And the light reaches all the way across.
